note: Maps which underlying capabilities matter in which domain, and proposes evaluation tailored to the domain rather than to a general benchmark.
title: Fundamental Capabilities and Applications of Large Language Models: A Survey
explain_beginner: Large language models are used successfully across many different fields, medicine, law, finance, software engineering, and more, but this survey points out something often overlooked, different jobs actually depend on different underlying skills the model has, not some single overall intelligence score. It sets out to name and organize these underlying capabilities and then map which ones matter most for which of nine specific fields it studies. The core argument is that a model's score on a generic test does not necessarily predict how well it will do at a specific real job, because that generic test may not measure the particular skill that job actually needs. For example, legal work might depend heavily on precise long document reasoning, while creative writing depends more on generating varied, novel content, and a single benchmark rarely captures both well. The survey's practical suggestion is to evaluate models against the skills a specific domain needs rather than a one size fits all leaderboard score.
explain_business: For any organization selecting a model for a specific business function, this survey's practical takeaway is to stop treating a high score on a general benchmark like MMLU as sufficient evidence a model will perform well on your actual task, and instead identify which specific capability your use case depends on, precise document reasoning for legal or compliance work, numerical consistency for financial analysis, or code correctness for software tasks, and test specifically for that. This directly affects procurement and vendor evaluation now, since it gives buyers a concrete reason to request task specific evaluation results from vendors rather than accepting general leaderboard rankings as proof of fitness for a specialized deployment. The framework is domain general rather than tied to one industry, so it applies whether the deployment is in healthcare, legal services, or financial analysis, provided the buyer first identifies which underlying capability actually drives success in their specific use case.
explain_practitioner: This survey systematically documents large language models' fundamental capabilities, their formation mechanisms, and how these capabilities interrelate, then maps them onto nine application domains, medicine, law, computational biology, finance, social sciences and psychology, software engineering, robotics and agents, science more broadly, and creative work. Its central methodological contribution is an explicit mapping between named capabilities and the specific requirements of each domain, used to argue that standard aggregate benchmarks systematically misalign with real world task performance because the capabilities a benchmark measures are often not the ones a given deployment actually depends on. Rather than proposing one new evaluation, the survey's recommendation is domain tailored assessment, selecting which capabilities to test for a given deployment context based on that domain's actual requirements rather than defaulting to general leaderboard performance as a proxy for readiness in every field.
